title: Five loaves by the lake (Matthew 14:1–21)
hookLine: why does a story about feeding a crowd begin at a grave?
tomorrow: why do you start to sink the second you look down?

lines: AWFUL NEWS, AND A BUZZING PHONE.
A PICNIC THAT STARTS AT A GRAVE.
cards: You've had awful news and you just want to be alone. Then your phone lights up: someone else needs you, right now. Matthew has a story that sits exactly there, and it comes with a puzzle.

Why does a picnic for thousands start with a death? A gentle warning for anyone listening with kids: it's told in one short line. John, the man who baptized Jesus, has been killed in prison by Herod the tetrarch.
His friends bury him and come to tell Jesus.

teach.b: Matthew's next line: "When Jesus heard of it, he departed thence by ship into a desert place apart." Apart. Away from everyone.
But the crowds hear where he's gone and follow on foot, and when he lands, the quiet place is full.
Here's the hinge: "And Jesus went forth, and saw a great multitude, and was moved with compassion toward them, and he healed their sick." Nothing says the grief is over. The compassion comes anyway.
By evening, the disciples have a sensible plan: send everyone off to buy food.
He says: "They need not depart; give ye them to eat." Their answer: "We have here but five loaves, and two fishes."
He has the people sit on the grass, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives the bread to the disciples, and the disciples give it to the crowd.

Notice whose hands carry it: the friends who wanted to send everyone home. And the ending: "they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full." So, the puzzle.
Why open a feast at a grave? Matthew sets them side by side, with no gap between.
On the same day, in the same person, grief and compassion share the room. One doesn't have to finish before the other begins.

how: Some churches bring meals to grieving families, and some Christians say grace before meals with thanks for the hands that brought the food, remembering loaves broken and shared.

games.q: what does “five loaves by the lake” mean?
o: a meal Jesus kept for his own disciples
a little bread, shared on a day of grief
the bread used at the temple's festivals

p: where he went on hearing of John

s: Jesus handed every piece of bread to the crowd himself
he gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.
Matthew places the feeding right after news of John's death

games.q: you just got hard news. an hour later a friend texts: can you help me move tomorrow? what fits the lakeside story?
o: say no; grief means you have nothing to give right now.
say yes and hide that anything is wrong.
help a little, honestly, and tell them you're sad.
games.why: Jesus withdrew apart first, and then, seeing the crowd, was moved with compassion. in Matthew, grief and compassion share the same day; neither cancels the other.

practice: Name one person who could use something from you this week. Then name what might stop you: a low mood, a long day, your own sad news.
Now choose the smallest version you could still give on a hard day, five loaves rather than a banquet, and hold that plan while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Five loaves by the lake. Not much to start with, broken and handed out by the disciples, on the day John was buried.

orig.note: Greek for to be moved with compassion, the verb in Matthew 14:14.

carryVoice: Your line: compassion in grief. Sadness doesn't have to clear the room before kindness walks in. Take care.
